title: What State Standards Look Like on the NAEP Scale September 17, 2026
author: Amber M. Northern
source: Thomas B. Fordham Institute, Education Gadfly Weekly review (fordhaminstitute.org),
summary: Amber Northern reviews NCES's ninth Mapping State Proficiency Standards report, which places each state's 2022 proficiency cut scores for fourth- and eighth-grade reading and math onto the common NAEP scale so that otherwise incomparable state expectations can be compared. She explains that because states must participate in NAEP in these grades, the exercise functions as an external audit of state expectations beyond any state's control. The findings show that only Illinois, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island set standards equivalent to NAEP Proficient in both subjects and grades, that most states cluster at NAEP Basic, and that Iowa and Virginia fell below Basic in reading; changes since 2019 were mostly modest, with some states rising and others slipping. Writing partly as a Virginia state board member, Northern acknowledges the debate over whether NAEP Proficient or NAEP Basic is the right target. Her interpretive move is that the value of the crosswalk is not an immediate leap to NAEP Proficient but a transparent common scale that shows states how much room remains to raise expectations, ideally through a phased approach.
points: Mapping state cut scores onto NAEP's 0 to 500 scale turns NAEP into an external audit of state expectations, since states cannot control or opt out of the grade 4 and 8 reading and math assessments.
In 2022 only three states (Illinois, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island) set proficiency bars equivalent to NAEP Proficient across both subjects and grades.
Iowa and Virginia set reading standards below NAEP Basic in both grades, a result Northern says is motivating serious work on Virginia's state board.
Movement since 2019 was mostly upward in reading and grade 4 math but churned in grade 8 math, where Massachusetts and Arizona fell from Proficient to Basic.
Northern argues the crosswalk's real use is showing states how far their expectations sit below a common benchmark, supporting phased increases rather than an overnight jump.
quotes: Since standards vary across states, the results of state assessments can’t be used to directly compare students’ progress from place to place. But by placing a state standard or cut score onto the NAEP scale, which is a common metric, a NAEP-equivalent score of that standard can be generated and compared across states.

Because states are required to participate in NAEP reading and math in grades 4 and 8, the assessment also serves as an external audit of state expectations—one that sits beyond any individual state’s control.
Only three states were equivalent to NAEP Proficient in both subjects and both grades in 2022—Illinois, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island.

Two states—Iowa and Virginia—had standards below NAEP Basic. (Make no mistake that the Old Dominion’s unacceptable standing on this metric is motivating serious work from those of us on the state board!)
There was more churn observed in grade 8 math as, for example, Indiana and Oklahoma rose from Basic to Proficient, while Massachusetts and Arizona fell from Proficient to Basic.

Reasonable people can debate, and many have, whether NAEP Proficiency is best understood as a college-ready benchmark and, similarly, whether NAEP Basic is the more appropriate target for all students.
It is that states can easily compare where their standards sit on a common scale and see how much room there is to keep raising expectations.
